headline: Senate blocked a bill that would have set federal rules for companies issuing payment stablecoins, a type of digital currency tied to a fixed value.
what_it_does: The bill would have allowed only approved companies to issue payment stablecoins for people in the U.S., with fines up to $1 million and up to 5 years in prison for knowing violations. Issuers would have had to back each coin one-to-one with U.S. dollars or similar safe assets, publish monthly reserve reports, and disclose how people can cash out their coins. Smaller issuers (up to $10 billion) could choose state oversight instead of federal oversight. Approved stablecoins would not have been treated as securities or commodities, but issuers would have had to follow anti-money laundering rules.

who_it_affects.how: They would have needed federal or state approval, full one-to-one reserves, monthly public reserve reports, and anti-money laundering programs.

who_it_affects.group: People who buy, hold, or use stablecoins
who_it_affects.how: They would have gotten required public disclosures on reserves and redemption, and certain priority for their claims if an issuer went bankrupt.

who_it_affects.group: Crypto exchanges and other digital asset service providers
who_it_affects.how: Three years after enactment, they would have been barred from offering stablecoins not issued by approved issuers or by foreign issuers that meet the bill's requirements.
Their subsidiaries could have applied to issue stablecoins under federal supervision.
They could have sold stablecoins in the U.S. only if Treasury found their home country's rules comparable, they registered with the OCC, and they held enough reserves in U.S. institutions.

who_it_affects.group: Large public companies outside the financial industry
who_it_affects.how: They would have been barred from issuing stablecoins unless a federal review committee unanimously approved.
They would have had to report holdings of approved stablecoins worth more than $5,000 on their financial disclosure forms.
